record.title: Terminal-Bench audit reports task defects and budget effects that change agent scores
record.summary: A 5 November arXiv paper describes a continuous audit workflow and the Terminal-Bench 2.1 update to Terminal-Bench 2.0. The authors report repair issues in 28 tasks, score increases over 10 percentage points, changes of up to three leaderboard places and a 19-agent rank correlation of 0.958; they also report that extended time budgets shrink some fixed-budget harness gaps. The audit combines task files, execution traces, community reports, automated checks and maintainer-reviewed repairs. Its workflow precision/recall are retrospective because it helped construct the repair set. The linked public repository is accessible and lists an Apache-2.0 license, but its README says 26 tasks were modified, which does not match the paper’s 28-task count. Results are author-reported and were not independently reproduced here.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: A 5 November 2026 arXiv preprint describes the Terminal-Bench 2.0 audit and Terminal-Bench 2.1 release. The linked public Harbor repository contains task, configuration and leaderboard directories and lists an Apache-2.0 license.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that their audit identified repair issues in 28 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, about one third of the benchmark, including 14 tasks they say were newly identified by their process. They report that benchmark accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points after repair, some leaderboard positions changed by up to three places, and the overall 19-agent ranking correlation was Spearman rho 0.958.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report that more than half of failed Terminal-Bench trials ended in timeouts under default budgets. In a higher-time-budget analysis, extending wall-clock budgets substantially reduced some fixed-budget harness gaps, including a reported roughly 20 percentage-point GPT-5.4 gap and a 30-to-5-point GPT-5.4-mini gap. These results depend on the stated harness, task and model configurations.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report 57.1% precision and 71.4% recall for their audit workflow against the final TB2.1 repairs, but state that the workflow contributed to constructing that repair set; these are retrospective agreement metrics rather than independent defect-discovery estimates. On a separate 34-task Harbor-Index sample, the authors report 12 confirmed defects among 14 flagged tasks, with manually reviewed cases including defects the workflow missed.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper and repository README do not report the same task count: the paper says 28 tasks surfaced or needed repair, while the current repository README says 26 tasks were modified. This check did not reconcile the counts or independently rerun the task-level repairs and model comparisons.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The results do not establish how often agent benchmarks generally contain defects, nor do they isolate model capability from harness, environment and resource settings beyond the paper’s tested Terminal-Bench and 34-task Harbor-Index samples.

evidence_gaps.description: The 28-task paper repair set and the repository README statement that 26 tasks were modified have not been reconciled task by task.
The benchmark repair and resource-sensitivity results have not been independently reproduced.
The reported 57.1% precision/71.4% recall measure agreement with a repair set the workflow helped construct, not independent defect discovery.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported effects reproduce, the audit shows that defects and budget choices in a prominent coding-agent benchmark can materially change absolute scores and some relative rankings. It can change how agent capability claims and evaluation infrastructure are compared, without proving a general defect rate across benchmarks.
limitations: Results are from one author-led audit of Terminal-Bench 2.0 and a 34-task Harbor-Index external-validity sample; neither establishes benchmark-wide defect prevalence.
The reported workflow precision and recall are retrospective because the workflow contributed to constructing the final repair set; agreement with that set is not independent discovery accuracy.
The paper reports 28 tasks surfaced or requiring repairs; the current linked repository README says 26 tasks were modified. This count difference is unresolved.
No independent task-level rerun or score reproduction was performed in this activation.
Terminal-Bench 2.1 is publicly available, but its artifact existence does not by itself validate the paper’s model scores or audit conclusions.
brief.summary: A 5 November arXiv paper describes a continuous audit workflow and the Terminal-Bench 2.1 update to Terminal-Bench 2.0. The authors report repair issues in 28 tasks, score increases over 10 percentage points, changes of up to three leaderboard places and a 19-agent rank correlation of 0.958; they also report that extended time budgets shrink some fixed-budget harness gaps. The audit combines task files, execution traces, community reports, automated checks and maintainer-reviewed repairs. Its workflow precision/recall are retrospective because it helped construct the repair set. The linked public repository is accessible and lists an Apache-2.0 license, but its README says 26 tasks were modified, which does not match the paper’s 28-task count. technical.claimed_result: The authors report issues requiring repair in 28 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks, over 10 percentage points aggregate score increase after repair, up to three ranking positions changed, and Spearman rho 0.958 across 19 evaluated agents. They report default-budget timeouts in over half of failed trials and reduced selected harness gaps when wall-clock limits were extended.
technical.demonstrated_result: The arXiv paper and its workflow/results are directly inspectable, and its linked public Harbor repository contains a Terminal-Bench 2.1 task/config/leaderboard tree under an Apache-2.0 license. This activation did not independently reproduce scores or validate task repairs.
technical.mechanism: An evidence collector gathers static task materials, execution traces and community reports; an auditor assigns evidence-backed defect categories and proposes repairs; an independent verifier checks evidence and runs the reference solution; maintainer review gates final changes. The paper classifies instruction–verification mismatch, task drift and environment/resource issues.
technical.regime: Terminal-Bench 2.0 audit: 89 tasks, 28 tasks reported as needing repair, and evaluation across 19 agent configurations. Resource sensitivity included wall-clock budgets up to 32 times default on a subset. External-validity study manually reviewed 34 tasks from an 80-task Harbor-Index snapshot. All quantitative outcome results are author-reported.
technical.reproducibility: The paper links a public benchmark repository, task-level revisions and supporting discussions; the repo README says 26 tasks were modified, while the paper says 28 tasks surfaced/needed repair. No independent comparison of those counts or task-level reproduction was performed here.
technical.strongest_baseline: Terminal-Bench 2.0 under its default protocol is the direct version baseline; the paper also compares selected harnesses at the standard time budget and at extended budgets. Comparisons remain specific to the paper’s tested agents, tasks, versions and resource settings.

brief.title: Terminal-Bench audit reports task defects and budget effects that change agent scores
brief.why_it_matters: If reproduced, the findings show that executable benchmark defects and chosen time budgets can change reported agent scores and some ranking conclusions. The paper makes benchmark upkeep a continuing measurement problem, while its own audit metrics are partly retrospective and the linked repository’s 26-task README count differs from the paper’s 28-task repair account. Independent task-level checks are needed before treating the reported score shifts as established.
